Chapter 2: The Deep Roots of Capital and Its Power
Think about the stories your family tells—maybe about lost fortunes, tough times, or a lucky break that changed everything. These tales aren’t just about your own relatives. They’re part of something bigger, a pattern that stretches across generations and continents. The way wealth builds up, and the power it brings, has always helped set the rules for how society works.
Let’s step back to the 19th century. Back then, the world was sharply divided by who owned what. In places like France and Britain, a small group of people held almost all the land and capital. And their wealth wasn’t just sitting in some account—it was land, factories, and businesses that kept pumping out money year after year.
For most folks, the only way to get by was to work for wages. Moving up the ladder? That was almost impossible. The gap between those who owned things and those who didn’t wasn’t just wide—it shaped everything, from who people married to how politics played out.
The numbers really say it all. In some countries, the richest 10% owned as much as 90% of all the wealth. The middle class was tiny. The poor, for the most part, had almost nothing. And inheritance? It was huge. Your future depended a lot more on who your parents were than on how hard you worked. If you’ve ever read a Jane Austen novel, where marriage is all about money and careful matchmaking, you’re getting a glimpse of how things really worked back then.
But here’s something to pay attention to—this system wasn’t just unfair, it was unstable. When wealth and power are locked up by just a few, resentment starts bubbling under the surface. It’s no surprise that political movements pushed for change, sometimes even leading to revolutions or sweeping reforms. Still, even when the laws shifted, the logic of capital stayed the same. Money, once it’s gathered, tends to grow. Investments make returns, and those returns can be invested again, like a snowball rolling downhill.
Then came the Industrial Revolution. Suddenly, factories and machines started creating whole new fortunes. Some workers did manage to climb up, but the basic pattern stuck around. If you could invest in these new industries, you made out best. The gap between owners and workers stayed stubbornly wide, even as the economy boomed.
Sometimes, though, big shocks broke this cycle. World Wars wiped out old fortunes, and governments had to step in to rebuild. High taxes on the rich, new social programs, and a push for equality all helped level the playing field. For a while, the gap shrank. More people started to believe in that dream—if you worked hard, you could build a better life.
But here’s the thing: these changes didn’t last. As economies bounced back and grew, old patterns crept back in. Inheritance started to matter more again, and wealth became more concentrated. The basic rule—the idea that capital, left on its own, tends to grow faster than the whole economy—just wouldn’t go away. Most people didn’t spot the shift right away. Maybe it was a jump in house prices, or student debt piling up, or just a feeling that some opportunities were quietly slipping out of reach.
So, what’s the real story of capital? It’s not just about money. It’s about power—the power to shape the future, to influence politics, and to write the rules. When wealth collects in a few hands, so does power. And that affects everything: who gets elected, what laws get passed, and which doors open—or stay closed. The deep roots of capital run through every part of society, shaping our lives in ways we often don’t even see.
